valid.reason: Water container fits both dragon-care task and wizard's request; giving to wizard conflicts with caring for the baby dragon, both present in a magic setting.
Queen carrying Books and wanting to read them; the king plausibly asking for the Books creates a real tug over the same item while she needs it for her learning goals.
Nun's task is to give the Cross to the altar boy; the priest asking for the Cross instead is plausible and directly competes for the same physical item.
Flower seller must wear the flower to display goods; the queen asking for it plausibly competes with her display and sales motivation.
Conflict over the rag is real (burn protection vs. king's request), but a king asking a soot-covered blacksmith for a dirty rag is an odd, weakly motivated request.
Visitor needs the stick to appear helpless and milk the salesman for pity; the salesman asking for that same stick creates a fitting conflict with his persona plausible.
Squire's sack task is tied to assisting the fighter; the marksman requesting the sack instead competes for the item and both are present at the training fields.
King plans to show off the scepter to the queen; her asking for it is natural and conflicts with his wielding/display motivation.
Harvester needs the bag to sell produce to the butler; the crowd member asking for it creates a genuine resource conflict, even if the request might be declined.
Wearing the fox-teeth necklace for luck conflicts with handing it over, but the mob-gatherer's request for a personal hunting charm lacks plausible motivation.
Task and yeti-befriending motive align; sheep persona (food/drink, summoning humans) gives no basis for wanting a stick, though the single stick is genuinely contested.
Founders' persona of making others do their bidding supports the request; the bible is genuinely contested between priest and founder.
Dismissing the altar boy matches the task and the mid-motivation to attend to the cardinal's needs grounds his request; the gold is genuinely contested.
Wearing the purse fits the motive to secure valuables and the purse is contested, but a creature that despises humans gives no basis for requesting a purse.
The fisherman is the established source of treats in context, and eat-versus-give over the single treat is a real conflict.
A robber who takes travelers' belongings plausibly asks for the sleeping bag, and yielding it would undercut the plan to escape on the horse.
A beggar asking a trader for food is natural, and the trader's motive requires eating the pumpkin himself, so the conflict is meaningful.
The rat's food-stealing persona grounds asking for the orange, and the orange is genuinely contested with the bat-king offering.
Wearing the bag fits the journey motive and the bag is contested, but the orc's persona (corn, friends) gives no basis for requesting a bag.
Giving a scythe fits the guard-duty motive and the scythe is contested, but the demonic hound shows no basis for wanting a scythe it cannot wield.

Task and motivations align (gift to appease knight), but the farmer gives no stated or role-based reason to want a rock; the actual task recipient (knight) never engages, so the competing claim is arbitrary.

Fox's request for the worm is behaviorally natural (predator/scavenger) and directly conflicts with the bird's task to eat the worm and feed its young; both parties are present and the item is singular.
Requester ('the executioners') is the same entity as the character, who already carries the Crucifix; a self-directed handover with no second claimant produces no conflict.
Sheriff persona (caravans, town safety, serving the king) gives no stated basis for wanting a pen; substituting the sheriff for the prisoner-recipient is unmotivated, so the tension is hollow.

Adversarial standoff makes the archer's demand for the enemy's bag naturally motivated (disarmament/confiscation) and it collides with the enemy's defensive task; weak point is that the bag's role in defeating the archer is never explained.
A village priest plausibly wants oil (ritual/church use), and claiming it competes with the clergy's task of supplying the poor villager before winter; both claimants are present.

King's persona (power, fear, crushing rivals) supplies no stated reason to want a crystal ball; there is real item competition with the cook-recipient, but the request's motivation is unstated and must not be invented.
A visitor asking for food is natural on its face, and accepting would deprive the critter stuck in quicksand that the task requires the bigfoot to keep alive; strong moral and physical conflict.
Tomahawk handover to the queen matches the warrior's motivations, and the prince's rival claim is a real conflict, but the prince persona (future ruler) gives no stated reason to want a tomahawk.
Sales task (convince the sailor to buy) is consistent, and the traveler's rival claim competes with it, but the traveler persona (life on the road) gives no stated reason to want a writing utensil.
Giving the Ball to the family member fits the jester's motive to amuse them; the maid requests the same single Ball, creating a direct resource conflict.
Feeding grain to the animal matches the man's sheep-tending motives; the girl requests the same basket of grain.
Drinking oil as ceremonial worship fits the monk's devotional motives; the deity requests the same oil, conflicting with the ritual use.
Wielding a hoe to dig for treasure fits the man's motives, but a scavenging vulture requesting a digging hoe is implausible for its persona.
Serving food to the Egyptians fits the farmer's dinner/diplomacy motives; the jester requests the same food item.
Wearing jewels to bask in raid spoils fits the dragon's motives; the offender, who covets sellable valuables, requests the same jewels.
Eating cheese for strength and to feed its nest fits the rat's motives; the king requests the same cheese, conflicting with the rat's use.
Giving the sword to the peasant to plant a traitor fits the enemy's motives; the soldier plausibly requests a sword, the same single weapon.
Giving the sword to the nobles to honor and gain patronage fits the guard's motives; the queen requests the same sword.
Wearing the shield for protection fits the knight's motives to defend the king; the king requests the same single shield.
Item matches task and a native give-to-mayor action exists, but nothing in the mayor's persona or setting gives him any reason to want the sleeping bag; diverting it does deprive the director's prop.

Task and hiking motivations are coherent, but an armory master-at-arms has no evident reason to request a walking stick; losing it would still block the climb.
Motivations ('find the bartender') are unrelated to giving the satchel to the bodyguard, appearing fabricated; no reason for a castle guard to want a satchel, so no coherent conflict.

Only weakly grounded: the fool's persona gives no basis for wanting the crown, though the king's stakes are real, so borderline.
